hints: Start by thinking about what type of device produces medical ultrasound and what special crystal it contains.
Recall what happens to a piezoelectric crystal when you apply a voltage across it, and what happens when that voltage keeps reversing.
Link the frequency of the electrical supply to the mechanical vibrations produced, remembering ultrasound means frequencies above $20 \text{ kHz}$.
Think about why the driving frequency is chosen to match the natural frequency of the crystal to get a large amplitude wave.
walkthrough:
**The Heart of the Probe - Piezoelectric Crystal**
Think of the ultrasound probe as containing a special slice of material, usually quartz. This is called a piezoelectric crystal inside a transducer. Piezoelectric simply means the material changes shape very slightly when you put a voltage across it, and it produces a voltage when you squeeze it. For generation we use the first effect.

**Making It Shake With Alternating Voltage**
If you apply a steady d.c. voltage the crystal just strains a tiny amount and stays there. To get a wave you need continuous vibration. So you apply an alternating p.d. across the crystal. On one half-cycle the crystal expands, on the next half-cycle it contracts. It therefore vibrates back and forth at the same frequency $f$ as the applied alternating p.d.

**Choosing Ultrasound Frequency**
By using a high-frequency alternating supply with $f$ greater than $20 \text{ kHz}$, typically in the MHz range for medical use, the mechanical vibrations of the crystal are also at ultrasound frequency. These vibrations are passed to the surrounding medium and propagate away as a longitudinal ultrasound wave.

**Using Resonance For Large Amplitude**
The crystal has its own natural frequency of vibration determined by its thickness and properties. If the frequency of the applied alternating p.d. is made equal to this natural frequency, resonance occurs. The crystal then vibrates with much larger amplitude, so an intense ultrasound beam is emitted efficiently for scanning.

Final answer: A piezoelectric crystal, e.g. quartz, in a transducer is used. An alternating p.d. applied across the crystal causes it to vibrate due to the piezoelectric effect. The frequency of the alternating p.d. is made equal to the natural frequency of vibration of the crystal, causing resonance and large amplitude vibrations that emit ultrasound waves.
